newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major dubious about Holocaust denial law.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major dubious about Holocaust denial law.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Tuesday indicated he was sceptical about proposals made recently by British parliamentarians for a law under which denial that the Holocaust took place would become a criminal offence.
"It might be right to have a specific offence... but I think I am dubious as to the practical effect of doing so," Major said in answer to a question in parliament from a Conservative MP.

On January 29, MPs indicated their support for a specific Holocaust denial offence, such as exists in some other European countries, by approving the introduction of a bill by Labour legislator Michael Gapes.
On the same day, Labour leader Tony Blair said there was "a very strong case" for such a law.

But Major said he was worried that printed material denying the mass killing of the Jews in World War Two could proliferate if its authors knew they would be showered in the publicity of a criminal trial.

He said there was no doubt the Holocaust was an historical fact. "I can understand the hurt and the offence and distress of those people who suffered or whose families suffered at that time (about its denial)," he said.

But he added: "I understand there is not a unanimous view in the Jewish community about this matter, and before I reached a conclusive view on it I would wish to take the view of those who are most concerned with this matter."

Gapes' bill has no chance of becoming law ahead of a British election due by May 22, and any bill to make Holocaust denial an offence would probably need the backing of the government elected then in order to become law.
